subject: steamLocomotive
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: 4-4-0 American steam locomotive.
Style: lithographed tinplate toy.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a tinplate-style 4-4-0 steam locomotive as a TypeScript module, considering whether to add rotating wheel joints via a root "body" joint or keep the model purely static given it's a vehicle rather than a creature.

For scale, I'm going with real-world size—locomotive plus tender around 16 meters total—rather than toy-scale, keeping the lithographed tinplate aesthetic but chunky realistic proportions. I'm orienting the model to face +Z with the locomotive front forward and tender trailing at -Z, centered on x=0.

Now I'm sketching the actual dimensions: track gauge gives wheel positions at roughly x=±0.72, with driver wheels around 0.85m radius and smaller pony/tender wheels near 0.45m. I'm laying out the body along z—pilot at the front, boiler as a horizontal cylinder around 1.5-1.6m diameter at cab height, smokebox slightly larger and painted black just ahead of it, leading into the smokestack placement.

I'm placing the diamond stack and headlight atop the smokebox, adding bell-shaped sand and steam domes along the boiler top, and now working out where the cab, firebox, and driver wheel pairs sit relative to the leading pony truck—roughly spacing the drivers about 2 meters apart with the pony truck out front.

I'm placing running boards above the drivers at y=2.0, running from z=-0.6 to z=6, sitting outside the wheels with clearance for wheel splashers in the classic 4-4-0 style.

I'm placing the cylinders outside the frame near the front, checking clearance against the pony truck wheels, and working out which driver axle the main rod connects to on a typical 4-4-0 layout.

I'm figuring out the crank pin angle for the rest pose, positioning the crosshead and main rod geometry so they align correctly with the forward driver.

I'm checking clearances between the pony wheels and cylinders, then working out the crank pin position and rod geometry so the crosshead, rod, and cylinder axis all line up properly at x≈0.98.

I'm working out the pin geometry so the side rod and main rod sit at slightly different x-offsets to avoid overlapping on the crank pin, with the pin extending out from the wheel face. Then I'm thinking about how to construct the wheel itself, likely as a disc with spokes.

Writing lathe profile for tire...

With 96 spokes across 4 wheels I'm worried about hitting the part limit, so I'm thinking of merging each wheel's spokes into a single geometry instead of individual parts, building a helper that constructs the spoke pattern in world-aligned coordinates to avoid orientation headaches.

For wheel rigging, each axle gets one joint aimed along +X with wheels on both sides rotating together, while rods stay rigidly attached to the chassis bone in rest pose.

I'm laying out the joint hierarchy: a root chassis joint at [0,1,0], with wheel joints (driverF, driverR, ponyF, ponyR) as children, then figuring out the tender's eight wheels across two trucks with axle positions along z, sizing the tender body length accordingly.

Now I'm working out exact axle z-positions for the tender trucks (-3.6, -4.6, -6.0, -7.0) with 0.45-radius wheels, and sketching the tender frame and tank body heights, leaving room for a coal pile on top.

I'm fleshing out the tender design: a boxy water tank with raised coal bunker walls at the front and a hatch at the rear, plus lithographed tinplate detailing like rivets, panel lines, painted lining, and fictional railroad lettering ("CENTRAL & WESTERN No. 7") rendered as SVG decals alongside headlight plates and builder's markings.

For the overall color scheme I'm going with a classic "General"-style 4-4-0 look: a deep forest green boiler with brass bands and domes, a black smokebox and balloon stack, vermilion red wheels with white-edged tires, a red pilot/cowcatcher, and the cab and tender finished in lithographed deep red-brown with yellow trim, including tiny printed engineer silhouettes in the cab windows for charm.

To sell the lithographed tinplate effect, I'm planning a paint function that layers warm highlights on top and cooler shading below, then adds random silvery scuff chips near the edges using noise thresholds to mimic worn paint revealing bare metal.

Now I'm mapping out the overall part structure and surface textures, starting with the tender side panel: a plane carrying "GRAND CENTRAL RAIL ROAD" lettering in gold with an ornamental border, and I'm working out how the plane's orientation and facing direction need to be set so the text reads correctly rather than mirrored when viewed from outside the tender.

Checking the other side confirms the same consistency: for s=-1 the local X axis also matches the viewer's right when seen from outside, so the orientation logic holds symmetrically on both sides. I'm now considering the reading direction of the text itself—on the +X side it reads toward -Z, meaning the loco's front appears to the viewer's left.

Next I'm planning the remaining textures: a cab side panel with the "No. 7" lettering and "ENGINE" text, window arches, and an engineer figure visible through the window on one side, mirroring that texture for the opposite cab side; plus a front number plate as a circular decal on the smokebox face.

I also want paint stripes along the boiler, a small fictional oval brass builder's plate ("TIN WORKS & CO. 1893"), and simple painted coal texture for the tender. I'll skip overly detailed wheel-spoke geometry and the clockwork-style pressure gauge since the cab backhead isn't realistically visible, but I'll add a soft glow effect for the headlight and cab windows.

I'm deciding to open the rear of the cab so the firebox door glows orange through it, using the glow kit for both the headlight lens and the firebox fire, with the cab roof and side windows intact but no rear wall. I'll make sure these textures load properly into the atlas so the glow effects render in their own colors, and I'm importing the glow kit module alongside the core builder API (joints, parts, sweeps, lathes, extrusions, rods, capsules, etc.) so I can construct the geometry carefully and avoid API errors.

Since the color palette is capped near 64 flat colors, I'm keeping my palette to roughly 30 named colors since paints don't count against that limit, and each color needs its own material. I'm writing a small helper function that wraps box geometry creation with a default bone attachment to the chassis, since un-anchored geometry snaps to whichever joint bone is nearest -- which risks parts accidentally attaching to a wheel joint instead of the body. I'm planning the tender as a separate root-level joint parented to the chassis, offset behind it, with its own truck joints underneath.

I'm also mapping out the smaller detail parts -- bell, whistle, sandbox, steam pipes, handrails, number plate, coupler, headlight -- and sketching the pilot (cow catcher) as an extruded wedge built from a triangular outline of slats running from the front tip back to the beam, extruded with thickness along the appropriate axes.

Still writing pilot slats...

Still sketching boiler geometry...

Actually I'll go with painted bands as lithography instead of extra geometry—cheaper and still reads as brass courses with pinstripe trim. Though tin toys often have embossed relief bands, so I'm considering adding lathe rings for a raised band profile around the boiler.

For dimensions, I'm placing the boiler centerline around y=2.4, with cab roof near 4.1 and stack top around 4.5, giving a realistic overall engine height near 4.3m. The smokebox sits forward as a black iron-grey cylinder with a front door dome including hinge straps, a central brass handle wheel, and maybe a number plate on the door face.

Above the smokebox I'm designing the headlight as a classic 1870s oil lantern -- a boxy body around 0.8x0.8x0.9 with a pyramid or cone roof, a ventilator knob, and a circular glowing front lens positioned above the boiler top near y=3.2, z=5.5.

I'm also planning the diamond stack with a lathe profile: a narrow base pipe flaring outward into a wide bell shape, then narrowing again toward a spark-arrestor cap, with a brass rim ring and small side position lamps alongside it.

Now I'm turning to the domes sitting on top of the boiler—a bell-shaped steam dome and a separate sandbox dome, each with their own smoothed lathe profiles and brass edge trim.

Settling sand dome at 3.3, steam dome at 2.0, whistle near 1.0 on top of the steam dome side. For the boiler, I'm figuring out how it extends from the visible front near the cab through to the hidden firebox section inside, with the backhead placed around z=-1.7 to keep the cab geometry consistent.

For the backhead I'll sketch my own gauge details rather than import anything, keeping things self-contained. I'm placing the cab floor at y=1.95 to sit above the driver splashers, with cab walls rising to 4.0 and a roof overhanging slightly to 4.2.

For the cab walls, instead of fighting with textured cutouts for the windows, I'll frame the openings with actual geometry—side pillars, a sill below, and a lintel above—leaving the window gaps open rather than faking glass with alpha transparency.

I'm also considering adding small figures inside the cab: an engineer leaning out one window and maybe a fireman on the other, each built from a torso box, sphere head, and a striped cap, with an arm resting on the sill for a toy-like touch.

For the cab itself, I'm placing a front wall with a small round opening for the boiler to pass through, overlapping where needed since it's hidden inside, and leaving the rear open but reinforced with two rear posts. For the roof, I'm thinking of a box shape with a raised clerestory strip and rounded eaves, possibly extruding a cross-section profile to get a slightly arched look rather than a flat lid.

Writing extrusion profile code...

For the roof finish, I'm leaning toward a pale cream base with brown line stripes to suggest painted wood planking, using a stripe pattern along the z-axis for the lined effect.

Now sizing the running boards: flat box per side running alongside the wheels with enough clearance above the 0.85-radius drivers, checking that the boards at y=1.95 clear the wheel tops comfortably. I'm skipping the splasher arches for simplicity and considering a thin vertical valence plate along the outer edge instead for visual detail.

For the frame, I'm placing main frame beams inside the wheel spacing at axle height running the length of the chassis, plus end cross-beams for the pilot and buffer beams where the boiler saddle will sit.

The running board at a higher elevation gets supported by thin stanchion brackets spaced every so often outside the wheels to keep part count manageable.

For the cylinder assembly on each side, I'm sweeping a cylindrical body shape along the length of the piece and capping the ends with brass disc-like heads.

I'm now adding the steam chest sitting atop the cylinder, sized to fit under the running board, plus cylinder cocks, a piston rod connecting to the crosshead, slide bars, and a main rod linking the crosshead to the driver's crank pin -- working through the geometry to get the pin positions and rod lengths roughly right relative to the wheel locations.

Checking that the crosshead and slide bar positions clear the front driver wheel's radius at that height, confirming there's enough space before adding simplified valve gear detail -- a rocker and thin eccentric rods running from the steam chest.

Now I'm moving to the tender: placing the front plate, draw bar coupling, frame sills, and tank dimensions, working out the box width, height, and length to sit properly behind the cab.

For the wood tender itself I'm thinking in tinplate style—a red-brown lithographed finish with side panel texturing. The top becomes a water tank deck with a filler hatch, and I'm adding a coal bunker at the front with raised wooden sideboards, giving it a sloped front wall toward the cab. For the coal pile I'm considering a faceted icosahedron mound, flat-shaded and scaled unevenly, with dark mottled paint and sparkle highlights to suggest coal.

Scattering individual coal lumps on top using low-poly spheres and small dodecahedrons, randomly placed around 25 pieces, merged into single geometries per color for efficiency. I'm sketching the tender body as a box roughly 2.6 wide, 1.35 tall, 5.2 long, then adding bunker walls on top—a sloped front wall and side walls with angled top edges, working out the extrusion directions so the thickness runs cleanly along one axis while keeping everything centered.

For the tender's trucks, I'm planning box-beam side frames with axle boxes, cylindrical axles spanning across, and wheels around 0.45 radius built as lathed tire profiles paired with disc hubs—trying to keep the lathe outline for the wheel simple rather than overly intricate with hub and rim details.

Still writing wheel profile...

For driver wheels I need spoked discs instead of solid ones, so I'm reworking the lathe profile for the tire to leave room for rods as spokes, plus a separate hub profile with its own lathe coordinates.

Still placing wheel geometry...

I'm working out the axle geometry—joints at the wheel center aiming along x, with a rod spanning from one wheel to the other sized with the right radius, bound to the axle bone. Then I'm starting to lay out the texture list needed for the model, aiming for at least five entries.

The first texture is a side panel SVG with gold border lines and lettering ("GRAND CENTRAL") in a serif font. The second is a cab panel with a gold number plaque, the third is a decorative window accent I decide to skip, and the fourth is a headlight lens with a radial glow effect, with a fifth texture still to be defined.

Continuing, I'm planning more plates: a brass smokebox numberplate for "7," an oval builder's plate decaled onto the curved boiler side (small, since the surface isn't flat), and possibly similar lettering for the tender's flat side. I still need gauge textures for the backhead, a glowing firebox door texture, and I'm considering whether the pilot needs one and whether to add a small facial texture (eyes, moustache, cap) for the engineer figure on a plane.

For the engineer's face, I'm deciding to use a plane decal facing sideways on the head sphere rather than a wrapped texture, since he should appear to be leaning out the side window looking toward the viewer. I'm skipping the headboard and smokestack textures, considering reusing the tender's rear lettering plate, and thinking about adding a pinstripe-bordered panel decal to the cab side wall around the window for a lithographed look.

Working out the SVG dimensions for the cab side litho sheet, positioning the window cutout and gold pinstripe borders relative to the wall frame...

Better to keep the sheet mostly transparent and just overlay gold double lines around the window frame, bottom panel, corner brackets, and the number "7", letting the box color show through everywhere else, with strokes thick enough to survive alpha testing at a 512px raster for a 300-wide texture.

For the tender, I'll paint the base box a deep red and add an overlay sheet with lettering, borders, rivet rows, and an embossed look, lifted slightly off the surface. To sell the lithographed tinplate feel, I want to add rolled bead details along roof and tender edges using thin rod geometry, plus crimped seams and rivets for texture.

Writing paint shader function...

I also need to confirm which helpers like paint, mix, smoothstep, noise, cells, rgb are actually exported from the SDK's main module, since everything should come from one import path.

I'm checking the resolution math for the paint atlas against the locomotive's overall surface area — a 1024 sheet spread across roughly 150 m² gives about 1.4 cm per texel, which seems workable for the level of detail needed.

Bumping to a 2048 paintSize gets things sharper, around 7mm per texel, which should be enough for rivets and other small details, while staying within the 4096 atlas limit. I'll keep flat colors for less visible areas like undersides and rods, reserving painted textures for the boiler, cab, tender, roof, and smokebox.

Now I'm setting up the core geometry constants — gauge width, driver radius, pony wheel radius, and trailing radius — to start defining the locomotive's physical dimensions.

Checking the z-positions for the pony wheels, cylinders, and drivers, the clearances all work out: the pony truck sits cleanly ahead of the front driver with an 18cm gap, and the rear driver clears the cab floor with wheels tucked below it. The cab overhangs the rear driver by about 1.8 units, which is typical for this kind of design, so the spacing looks consistent before moving on to the tender's front dimensions.

Now I'm working out the main frame geometry — its height, width, and z-extent relative to the axle positions, centering it at y=1.05 to sit properly above the drivers. Then I'm placing the running boards on each side, setting their width and vertical position, and checking how they align with the cab's side walls and extend along the boiler.

I'm defining the running board to run from the cab front to the front buffer beam, while the cab floor fills in the remaining area and width, then noting that the boiler's radius means it will intersect the floor slightly where it passes through the cab, which is fine since that part stays hidden.

Now I'm positioning the running boards so their inner edge clears the boiler's side profile, leaving a small gap, and setting their width and a slight upward lip for detail. For the cab walls, I'm placing them at the outer x boundary with some thickness, and figuring out where to cut the window opening along the side wall's length.

I'm dividing the cab side wall into sections along its length: a front pillar, the main window opening sized to about one unit wide, a rear pillar, and an open rear section mimicking the traditional open-side entry style of old steam locomotive cabs.

Still laying out wall posts...

I'm detailing the backhead with firebox door, gauges, and levers visible through the open cab rear, plus adding small seated engineer figures squeezed beside the boiler using simple torso and head boxes on narrow bench seats.

Working through sizing so the figure's head and cap clear the window opening, with torso and head positioned to peek through and a forearm resting on the sill.

Now I'm adding the boiler handrails with small stanchion rods connecting them at regular intervals, then moving on to the steam pipes sweeping from the dome down toward the cylinders.

Next I'm sketching the sandbox feed pipe and thin sand pipes running down toward the rails, then building the smokebox itself as a dark cylindrical sweep with a lathed front door profile, brass trim bands at both ends, and a numbered plate centered on the door face.

I'm also working out the headlamp placement on top of the boiler, figuring its box dimensions and vertical position before shaping its roof as a four-sided lathed pyramid with a small top vent.

Now I'm detailing the lamp lens with a circular textured glow, adding a brass ring around it using a lathed torus profile, plus side glass panels with glow and a bottom bracket, while making sure the lamp's front face stays behind the smokebox front plane.

I need to work out the front-to-back ordering of smokebox fittings: headlight should sit forward, stack behind it, then bell, sand dome, and steam dome further back. But checking the z-ranges, the stack's wide top risks overlapping the headlamp's footprint in both z and y, so I need to shift the stack's position or narrow its spread to avoid collision with the lamp.

Let me reposition everything with tighter spacing: shrinking the stack's flare radius and pulling it back slightly, then stacking the bell, sand dome, and steam dome in sequence further toward the rear with smaller radii so none of their footprints overlap.

I'm working out the boiler's taper and smokebox transition, placing boiler bands at intervals along its length and checking that the smokebox radius stays consistent with the boiler's front radius so the joint looks seamless.

Now I'm shaping the front pilot assembly, placing the buffer beam, coupler pocket, and cowcatcher as a triangular slat structure that tapers from wide at the rear to narrow near the nose.

Still writing slat positions...

I'm deciding to color the slats black iron with red cross bars, considering whether to add painted stripes to the buffer beam, and planning pilot support braces connecting to the frame plus a coupler piece.

For the remaining details, I'll keep brakes simple, add a cone-shaped spark arrestor cap to the chimney, and finalize sandbox, whistle and bell as basic shapes. I'm working out the cylinder geometry — placing the front head cap, brass disc dimensions, and checking that the steam chest radius and center height clear the boiler board above it.

Now I'm adding a visible steam pipe connecting the steam chest up to the smokebox side, plus a cylinder saddle bracket box bridging the frame to the cylinder mount, and starting on the pony truck bolster with side bars.

Still defining joint hierarchy...

Working out the tender's underframe details with side frames, springs, and axle boxes, plus a coupling draw bar and footplate connecting the loco cab to the tender, and planning the tender body's painted panel styling with raised frames and top rail beads.

Now I'm setting the tender box height and top deck, adding a round water hatch with a dome lid near the rear and a coal area bounded by a front coal board. I'm also settling on the classic tinplate color scheme—Tuscan red tender with gold stripes and cream panel lines, paired with a deep green boiler for that traditional toy train palette.

Picking final hex values: forest-green boiler, plum-black smokebox and frame, red-brown cab and tender, vermilion wheels with silver tires, brass and gold lining accents, cream roof, and a black pilot with a red beam and brass headlight.

Now I'm working out how to place rivet dots along the boiler seams using circumferential arc-length math, checking proximity to band centers and a rivet pitch so each rivet shows up as a small dot near the seams.

I also want matching rivet rows on the tender texture, soot-streaked black paint for the smokebox, and silvery flat tires for the wheels versus a reddish lathe tone, and I'm cataloging the full set of paint colors I'll need: green, red, black, cream, brass, and a few more.

Now I'm sketching out a helper function for building box-shaped parts with position, color, and bone attachment options, keeping the typing loose since precision isn't critical here.

Using `any` to sidestep the overload resolution for the part options. For the rod helper, I'll pass an explicit bone reference since the literal tuple points lack one and nearest-joint inference could pick the wrong joint. For the sides loop, s=1 maps to the left (+X) side per the model convention.

Writing builder imports...

Defining a tin-paint helper that blends highlight and shadow colors based on surface lighting, then layers in cell noise for wear patterns...

Writing boiler paint shader...

Still defining the paint patterns...

For the roof I'm adding cream paint with brown plank seams running periodically along x, darker tones on the underside, and for the coal I'm using a dark base color with occasional highlight glints and rare sparkle for realism. Now I'm moving on to setting up the tender texture canvas dimensions to match its real-world size.

Still writing SVG decoration code...

Still mapping cab texture coordinates...

Writing texture generation functions...

Mapping the window and panel bands into pixel coordinates, I'm now moving to the other textures: a brass-ringed number plate for the smokebox with a cream "7" on dark red, a glowing lens with radial gradient and fresnel rings, and a firebox door texture with a metal ring around a glowing flame-filled opening on the backhead.

For the gauge, I'll just reuse the tested gaugeTexture from the clockwork kit rather than drawing my own. For faces, I'm planning two small SVG textures — one for the engineer with a moustache and bushy eyebrows, one for the fireman with round cheeks and soot smudges — placed on planes in front of each head sphere.

Working out the placement geometry is tricky since the plane needs to sit close to the curved sphere surface without clipping or floating too obviously; I'm testing distances and radii to find a position where the disc mostly hugs the sphere, accepting some minor floatiness as fine for this toy-scale model.

Switching approach, I consider a faceted sphere with a flat face plane in front, or a box-shaped head where a texture showing "FACE" is applied to all six faces—simpler since hidden faces don't matter and texturing all sides is easy, even if slightly wasteful.

Now I'm designing a brass builder's plate decal reading "BUILT BY / TINWORKS / 1893" to apply onto the boiler surface, positioning it near the boiler's side around y=2.45 away from the handrails and sand dome so it doesn't conflict with other details.

Skipping extra decals on the smokebox and tender rear plate, and deciding against separate colored side lamp lenses, instead reusing a dimmed lens texture for the side glass panel. I'm tallying up the textures used so far—tender side, cab panels, numberplate, lens, fire, gauge, faces, builder plate, stripes—around ten or eleven total, and now considering a buffer beam texture with a printed number and diagonal warning stripe.

Now I'm sketching the buffer beam texture: a red field with white chevrons, gold border, and rivets, bringing the texture count to twelve, and confirming atlas sizing is reasonable across the different texture dimensions.

Moving into the geometry helper functions, I'm starting to define a wheel-set builder that takes an axle joint, z-coordinate, radius, and driver flag, figuring out how to type the Joint parameter from the SDK. For each side I'm planning to generate a lathed tire mesh positioned at the gauge offset and radius, oriented along the axle axis and bound to the axle bone with the appropriate paint color.

For the hub I'm using another lathe shape, and for driver wheels I'm working out spoke geometry: twelve thin radial boxes merged into one mesh, each computed by rotating a box around the X axis to position it at the right angle and radial distance, then translating it into place relative to the wheel center.

I'm also planning a crescent counterweight for drivers and accounting for the crank pin boss, while non-driver wheels get a simpler disc with dish, rim, and six outer ribs. Per driver wheel that's roughly four part types (tire, hub, spokes, counterweight) doubled for both sides, so eight parts per axle, plus I still need to add the axle rods and crank pins connecting the wheels.

Now I'm figuring out crank pin placement using the crank radius relative to axle height, and setting up joint bones for each wheel type (driver, pony) with their respective radii so they can rotate correctly. I'm also planning a small helper function for rolled bead edges and starting to tally up the total part count across the model.

Writing build function...

Still defining joints...

Child joints only need explicit dir when bone assignment matters; otherwise their world-space positions remain unaffected by parent orientation. I'm sketching helper functions for creating bones and geometry primitives inside the build routine.

Defining more helpers...

Still defining the boiler and smokebox geometry...

Now I'm building a ring helper for the boiler bands, lathing a small rectangular profile around the boiler radius at each band position, and checking whether lathe parts need to follow the chassis bone for rigidity.

I'm sketching the smokebox door as a lathed dome profile positioned at the end of the boiler, then adding a thin brass ring at the door's edge and planning the door straps next.

I'm figuring out the radial strap rods that curve across the dome's surface, running them from a point near the apex down to the rim, spaced around the circumference, plus a small center knob and a thin plate near the top to finish the detail.

Now I'm shaping the stack and spark arrestor as lathed profiles, building up the chimney-like silhouette with stepped radii before tapering into a small cone cap at the top.

Now I'm designing the headlamp group near the front: a small base stand, a black tin body with brass trim framing, and a circular lens disc positioned at the front face.

I'm sketching the roof as a lathe-generated pyramid shape with a square cross-section (using 4 segments), sized slightly larger than the body for overhanging eaves, and figuring out the rotation needed to align it properly.

Still defining dome geometry...

Thinking through the bell's lathe profile and yoke posts next, building out the bell shape with mounting rods.

Checking the inner and outer paths don't cross, then positioning the bell upright with mouth facing down, mounted under a yoke on top of the boiler at the right height.

I'm setting up a simple yoke with two posts connecting the bell to the boiler, adding a brass whistle cylinder with a cap sphere near the boiler top, and skipping the safety valve since the sandbox detail is already handled. I'm adding knob caps at the handrail ends and three stanchions connecting the rail down to the boiler surface, checking that the stanchion endpoints land just inside the boiler radius. Then I'm moving into the cab roof, defining its extrusion profile and positioning along the z-axis.

Writing extrude code...

Adding gold trim rods...

I'm adding a light-colored sill ledge and a glass sheet positioned over the cab window opening, then checking the gap between the cab rear and the tender front for the fall plate, before moving on to the firebox backhead where the boiler ends.

Checking torso and boiler positions to avoid overlap, then building the figure's torso box, spherical head, flat face circle, and cap cylinder.
